formulation:
Tammy is 54, works as not in workforce, alone.

How life is going overall. poor.

What brings them here now. Tammy Faison, 54, presents with low mood, loss of interest and energy, and poor sleep that have deepened since a falling-out with her sister two months ago ended the Sunday family dinners she had hosted for thirty years; she has since withdrawn from Thursday choir rehearsal, her Saturday church pantry shift, and karaoke and trivia nights. She was laid off from her community outreach role in the spring, describes a scattered job search — applications started and abandoned — and reports feeling constantly behind and 'running on empty,' though she is tearful mainly when describing the estrangement. She reports one similar period after her divorce seven years ago that lifted without treatment; she denies any thoughts of self-harm, denies drinking or using anything to cope, and says her health is fine.
What they want out of support: I want to be back at the Sunday dinner table with my family — to get through one meal with my sister without it turning into that night again, and without me pretending the whole time that I'm fine.

Predisposing. Tammy was the oldest of five in a house off Second Street, with a mother who cooked nights at the hospital and a father who drove a cab, so from eleven she had the Sunday kitchen and the younger ones — greens and fried chicken for nine, homework checked, the little ones kept off the porch steps in summer. Nobody asked how she was managing, because the answer was always fine; what got praised at the gatherings was the holding itself — that girl can feed a whole house — and by fourteen she was running the junior usher board besides. She took from all of it that her seat at every table in that family was earned by what she put on it, and that being the one everybody counted on was the whole of who she was for. She carried that straight into adulthood — the house everybody came to, the kitchen half the church knew, the phone that always picked up.

Precipitating. Tammy was laid off in April when the grant died at the North Side youth center where she had run outreach for eleven years, and she had been holding herself together on the family calendar — the Sunday dinners she'd hosted for three decades, the fall storytelling nights. Then at her sister Renee's birthday dinner in August, Renee suggested the cousins 'take turns hosting for a while, till you get back on your feet'; Tammy heard being managed where help was meant, told the whole table exactly how many dinners Renee had cooked for this family in thirty years — none — and left before the cake. The Sunday dinners have stopped altogether, she let Renee's first two calls ring out and hasn't been back to Thursday choir or her pantry shift since, and the family group chat now carries the holiday planning without her. What brought her to the phone in late October was the garden going to weeds and a week in which the only person she spoke to was the cashier at the Kroger on Chamberlayne.

Perpetuating. Her strategy is to vanish before anyone can watch her fail at being Tammy — out of the room, out of the story, needs kept offstage — and to settle herself alone in the dirt when she can manage it. It protects her pride and it starves her: the quieter the phone gets, the surer she is nobody was coming anyway, and the harder it gets to be the one who reaches out first.
- withdrawal: She stops showing up before anyone can see her struggle: she gave up her Saturday pantry shift with a story about her knee, quietly dropped Thursday choir rehearsal, and hasn't called anyone first since the birthday dinner — the family group chat fills up under her thumb and she answers with a thumbs-up. For someone who has run on rooms full of people her whole life the silence is starving her, but she keeps the phone face-up on the kitchen table and waits to see who comes looking.
- hiding_needs: With the people she does still see, she plays the capable Tammy: at Sunday service she is blessed and busy, just 'between things,' and she would sooner carry a plate over to a shut-in than let one person at that church find out she was laid off in April. Miss Odessa has gotten 'I'm just focused on the job search' three times now, and each time Tammy turns the subject to somebody else's business.
- self_soothing: On mornings she can make herself get out to the backyard beds with the gospel station on, an hour of weeding settles her enough to cook herself a real supper; but the collards went to seed in July, and more mornings she stands at the kitchen window looking at the plot, then carries her coffee back to the couch.

Protective. Her church still holds her — she has missed only two Sunday mornings since August, sitting in her regular pew even on the weeks she can't make herself stay for coffee hour. Miss Odessa, who runs the food pantry, noticed her Saturday gap and calls every Wednesday now, no questions asked, just talking through the shopping list, and her niece Camille texts a photo from the choir stand every Sunday afternoon. And she made this call herself: looked up counseling at her kitchen table one night in October and dialed rather than waiting for somebody to come asking.

situation.event: Early in the week, a card arrived in Renee's handwriting. Not a holiday card, not a birthday — just an envelope, a few lines inside: that she keeps picking up the phone, that she's sorry about the birthday dinner, that she misses the table. Tammy left it on the counter for two days without opening it. When she finally did she was standing at the kitchen sink, and she read it there, then carried it to the table and read it again. The word that lodged was 'table' — not 'you.' She set the card face-down on the table and left it there. The next morning she went out back with her coffee, stood looking at the garden beds — just weeds now, the collards gone since July — and came back inside without touching anything. She has not called or texted Renee back. The card is still on the kitchen table.

formulation:
Earl is 26, works as office or administrative support worker, alone.

How life is going overall. poor.

What brings them here now. Earl is a 26-year-old administrative assistant whose father died suddenly of a heart attack three months ago; since then he has stopped fishing, stopped shelving at the library, and describes his apartment — dishes, laundry, an electric bill paid late for the first time in his life — as 'slipping.' He reports his first-ever performance problems at work (mis-keyed spreadsheets, a double-booked conference room) and has quietly shelved the community college courses he was set to start this fall toward an office-manager role, but denies drinking more than usual, denies any thoughts of harming himself, and insists he is 'handling it.'
What they want out of support: I want to get my place and my work back in order, and to be able to call my mother back on a Sunday without pretending I'm fine.

Predisposing. Earl grew up in a house where love was measured in what got fixed and how little was wasted, and where nobody asked how you were doing because the answer was assumed from how hard you were working. When his grandfather died his junior year of high school, Earl spent three weekends in the garage sanding a cedar chest for his grandmother, delivered it without a word, and was told what a steady boy he was. He came out of that house knowing how to true a door and file a warranty claim, and having never once heard — or said — what a feeling was, out loud.

Precipitating. Three months ago, in late March, Earl's father died of a heart attack in his own driveway while clearing the last snow of the season — gone before the ambulance arrived, nothing said, nothing finished. Earl took one week off and has been at his desk every day since; what he stopped was everything else — he never bought his fishing license this spring, missing his first opener since he was eight, and the pine bookcase he was building for his father's fishing manuals sits half-sanded in the corner of his apartment. Through May, mistakes started surfacing in the spreadsheets he had kept clean for four years, a double-booked conference room made it onto his supervisor's calendar, and the registration deadline for the fall courses he'd planned toward office manager came and went unsigned. What finally sent him looking for someone to talk to was smaller than any of it: a late-fee notice on the electric bill — the first bill he had ever paid late — which he sat holding for the better part of an hour.

Perpetuating. Earl copes by retreating to wherever nothing can be asked of him and by working only the parts of the loss that come with steps — the paperwork got a spreadsheet, everything else got silence — which keeps him upright and keeps anyone who might have helped him at arm's length.
- withdrawal: He told the library coordinator he'd 'take the summer off' from shelving, lets his mother's phone calls ring through to voicemail and answers with a short text instead, and skips roughly half the Thursday-night games, telling the group work is busy.
- going_over_it: On the drive home he replays the last phone call — his father wanting to look at the trailer bearings that weekend, Earl saying he had the inventory count — running it back to find the thing he must have missed; at work it shows up as checking the inventory spreadsheet three times before sending it, which he never used to do.
- problem_solving: He has handled his father's affairs like a project — a color-coded spreadsheet of the accounts, the insurance, the truck's title transfer, every box checked and filed — and it is the one corner of the loss where he still functions cleanly; it just hasn't touched the dishes, or the bookcase, or anything that doesn't come with steps.

Protective. Work is the one place Earl is still fully himself: first in every morning, still the person who opens the jammed copier nobody else will touch, and his supervisor's word last month was a question rather than a warning, so the job itself is not in question. He is not as alone as he acts, either — his mother texts every Sunday and he does answer, briefly, and when he logs on for the Thursday game, Ray, a machinist he has played strategy games with for six years, has started messaging him on the off-nights, asking nothing, just checking he's still there.

situation.event: His mother called over the weekend. He let it ring. The next day at lunch he listened to the voicemail twice: she'd started going through the garage — his father's tools, the tackle box — and was asking whether Earl wanted to come up any weekend soon to take what he'd like before she sorted the rest. He typed 'not yet, sorry' and sent it without calling back. She replied that same afternoon; he hasn't opened it. Each night since he's come home, walked past the half-sanded bookcase in the corner, and gone to bed without eating.

formulation:
Tatiana is 31, works as receptionist or information clerk, unstable transitional.

How life is going overall. poor.

What brings them here now. Tatiana presents feeling unable to manage the pressures at work and home since an involuntary move four months ago left her and her husband in transitional housing, currently his mother's spare room. She reports dread before shifts, two scheduling errors she would not normally make, withdrawing from the evening class she had just enrolled in, and crying in her car before work; alongside this she questions whether the office-manager path she has worked toward is still what she wants, though she frames this as tiredness more than crisis. She denies any thoughts of self-harm and any increase in drinking, has not missed a day of work, and reports strain with her husband and mother-in-law but no rupture.
What they want out of support: I want to get through a week at work without crying in my car or dreading Monday, and to feel like I know what I'm working toward again.

Predisposing. Tatiana grew up in a mill house outside town, the eldest of three, with her father on second shift at the poultry plant and her mother waiting tables and picking up doubles whenever the paychecks came up short. By twelve she had supper on the stove and her little brother's homework checked, and nobody in that house ever had to ask — being the one who never needed anything was simply her place in it. Good was expected rather than celebrated, and her grandmother calling her 'the little mother' was the highest praise she got. She grew into an adult who met every bar set for her and never once counted meeting it as having done well.

Precipitating. Four months ago the duplex she and Jesse had rented for six years was sold out from under them — the new owner wanted the unit for family, and thirty days' notice was all the law required. Nothing they could afford in town came without first, last, and a deposit they didn't have, six weeks in an extended-stay motel ate most of what savings remained, and since spring they have been in his mother's spare room. Tatiana withdrew from the evening class she had finally enrolled in at the community college, put the sewing machine and her fabric stash into a storage unit, left her flowerpots with a neighbor, and stopped staying after church for coffee. She hasn't missed a day of work, but she cried in the supply room once, and twice now she has caught mistakes in the office schedule that she would never have made before.

Perpetuating. Her strategy is to control everything small and say nothing about what's big, which keeps everyone around her comfortable and keeps her alone with the whole of it. The overcontrol costs her sleep, and the hiding costs her the closeness to Jesse that might actually carry some of the weight.
- overcontrol: She manages whatever is left to manage: on Sundays she irons a week's worth of shirts for both of them, the storage unit is inventoried in a spreadsheet with every box numbered, and she keeps a three-ring binder of every rental listing within thirty miles with call-back dates highlighted in yellow. She works the binder on her lunch break, and it buys her twenty minutes of feeling capable — but it has yet to change what's in the deposit column, and it is always the first thing she reaches for instead of sleep.
- hiding_needs: When Miss Earline asks how they're settling in, she says getting on fine; when her sister texts 'you okay?' she sends back a thumbs-up; she cried in the supply room and told the office it was allergies. Jesse has started saying he feels like a boarder in his own marriage, because by the time his double shift ends there is nothing left for him to be told.
- self_soothing: She kept one project out of storage — a quilt top she is piecing by hand for the place they don't have yet — and on good nights she stitches on it in the living room after everyone's asleep, ten stitches at a time. On bad weeks the bag stays zipped, because it feels too much like planning for a home she can't give them.

Protective. She still has her pew on Sunday mornings and her Thursday evening shift organizing the senior lunches at the community center, and the people there would show up for her if she ever let them — Miss Earline has already offered the church's emergency fund twice. She is still, by everyone's account including her own, very good at her job: she can soothe an angry caller and untangle a double-booked schedule without breaking stride, and she trusts that about herself even now. And she booked this support herself, the first time in her life she has asked for help for herself instead of being the one who arranges it for everybody else, which she knows in her practical way must mean something.

situation.event: The fall semester started at the community college this week — the same one she'd enrolled in before the spring came apart. She drives that highway every morning, and on Monday the lot was full the way it hadn't been in months. She noted it and kept going. The week ran the same way weeks have been running: ironing Sunday night, the binder on her lunch break, calls routed and calendars managed at the front desk. On Thursday she was setting up for the senior lunch at the community center when Miss Earline asked how she and Jesse were getting on at his mother's. Tatiana said they were making it work. Miss Earline took her hand and said she meant it about the church fund, any time. Tatiana thanked her and said she knew. That night, after Jesse and his mother were in bed, she got the quilt bag down from the shelf in the spare room and carried it to the living room. She sat with it in her lap. She didn't open it. After a while she put it back.

formulation:
Kristine is 24, works as maid or housekeeping cleaner, unstable transitional.

How life is going overall. poor.

What brings them here now. Kristine is a 24-year-old hotel housekeeper presenting with just over two months of low mood following the loss of her apartment when her building was sold: she reports feeling flat and heavy most days, crying in her car after shifts, and abandoning the knitting, journaling, and yoga she previously used to steady herself. She describes trouble falling asleep most nights, typically lying awake until around 2 a.m. going over money and housing, running on four to five hours, and she has withdrawn from her friend group while rotating between a friend's couch, a cousin's spare room, and a weekly motel. She denies any thoughts of self-harm or suicide, denies alcohol or substance use, and insists her work is unaffected — clients still request her by name — though she concedes her days off have become 'pointless.'
What they want out of support: I want to sleep through the night again and have one evening a week where I actually pick up my knitting instead of just staring at the bag.

Predisposing. Kristine grew up in a brick house outside Loop 410 where Saturday morning cleaning was family law: her mother kept the kitchen like a showroom, and her father walked the garage floor checking for oil spots the way other dads checked report cards. Praise was quiet when it came at all, and it came for things done right, never for just showing up — a 94 on a test got asked about the missing six points. She learned early that being good at something only counted until the next thing needed doing, and by middle school she was re-scrubbing baseboards her mother had already approved.

Precipitating. Ten weeks ago the fourplex off Fredericksburg Road that Kristine had rented for three years was sold, and the new owners gave every tenant thirty days to be out — renovations, they said, though the units relisted within the month at four hundred dollars more. Nothing she found came close to what a housekeeper's paycheck could carry, so since late spring she has been rotating between her friend Deshawn's couch, her cousin's spare room in Converse, and a weekly motel on the Northwest Side, with most of what she owns in her Corolla. The fifteen hundred dollars she had saved toward her IICRC certification went to motel weeks and a deposit on an application that went nowhere. Since then she has stopped knitting and journaling, deleted the certification course from her bookmarks, skipped Fiesta for the first time since she was a kid, and bailed on three straight Catan nights, telling everyone she's basically sorted and almost locked in on a place.

Perpetuating. Her coping is an attempt to go on being the competent one in a situation that does not reward competence: control whatever can be controlled, show no needs, and review everything for the mistake that must explain it. It keeps her employed and presentable while it quietly costs her the rest — the yarn stays in the trunk, her friends get the stiff version of her, and the nightly audit is exactly what is eating her sleep.
- overcontrol: At work it pays — she runs her cart like a cockpit, and it is a big part of why the penthouse checkouts land on her. Everywhere else it runs her: she re-sorts the motel room every time she checks back in, keeps the Corolla detailed because it is the only space that is fully hers, and she was up at 5:40 one Sunday bleaching Deshawn's shower grout while he slept — the fight that followed is why they have been stiff with each other since.
- hiding_needs: Everyone gets the same answer — 'basically sorted, just finalizing a place' — including her parents, who hear from her every Sunday and know nothing about any of it; taking her dad's guest room would mean admitting the plan failed. The only place the true version of her week exists is the intake form she filled out at 2 a.m. in the motel parking lot.
- going_over_it: Sleep is when the audit runs: from midnight to two she goes over the day line by line — every dollar, every listing, every text and what it might have cost her — like a checklist that never closes out. The 4-7-8 breathing she learned in yoga still works on the nights she can make herself start it, but most nights the audit wins.

Protective. Work still runs the way it should: the boutique hotel downtown requests her by name for deep cleans, her cart is inventoried to the ounce, and new hires get told to watch how she turns over a room. She takes a flat, real pride in a streak-free shower door that ten weeks of motel living hasn't touched. And she got herself here — found this service alone at 2 a.m. on her phone, filled out every field, and showed up, which for a woman who would rather scrub a stranger's grout than ask a friend for a ride is not a small thing.

situation.event:
Ten weeks in, she had the rotation working — or working enough. Her cousin's spare room in Converse through the end of the week, motel after that, and a studio listing she'd been watching that sat just at the ceiling of what she could carry if she stretched.

Thursday evening her cousin came home and said it easily, apologetically: her partner was flying back earlier than expected, she'd need the spare room by tomorrow morning. No argument — just the way things go. Kristine said of course, not a problem, and had her bags in the Corolla before her cousin finished the sentence.

She didn't book the motel that night. It was two days early and she'd been trying to hold the rate off as long as she could. She drove to a parking lot off Loop 1604 and reclined the seat and lay there in the summer heat with the windows cracked, running the AC in short bursts so she wouldn't drain the battery. Before she tried to sleep she reorganized the back seat — moved the box with her certification materials to one side, straightened the bag with the yarn in it — the way she does every time the car becomes the room. She was up when the lot got loud.

In the morning she booked the motel. The weekly rate was up from last time. She paid it without looking at the total twice, then checked her phone on her first break and saw the studio listing had closed — someone else's application had gone through.

formulation:
Natalie is 18, works as not in workforce, unstable transitional.

How life is going overall. poor.

What brings them here now. Natalie is an 18-year-old first-year student presenting eleven weeks after the sudden death of her grandmother, Mom-Mom, from a stroke at seventy-one. She had been living in her grandmother's spare room since starting at Kutztown, and since the house was listed for sale she has been rotating between friends' couches with most of her belongings in her car; she cannot start or finish coursework, has stopped painting, and is avoiding her mother's calls. She is tearful describing clearing the bungalow but bright and quick about everything else; she denies any thoughts of harming herself, denies using alcohol or anything else to cope apart from what she calls a professionally dangerous amount of coffee, and has never sought mental-health support before.
What they want out of support: I want to be living in one place where I'm not counting down my welcome, and to get through a normal week — class, painting, calling Mom — without spending half of it dodging everything.

Predisposing. Natalie had done a version of this once before, and nobody noticed. The October she was fifteen, her Pop-Pop died of a heart attack, and for most of that school year she stopped painting, ate lunch alone in the art room, and did her homework at two in the morning — while at church suppers and Sunday dinners she stayed Natalie: funny, helpful, first to clear the plates. Grown-ups kept telling her mother how well she was taking it, and she took that on as the job. What she learned was that getting through it looked like keeping everyone else comfortable while she came apart quietly, on her own schedule.

Precipitating. Eleven weeks ago, in the first week of March, Natalie's grandmother — Mom-Mom, the one who taught her acrylics at the kitchen table and whose spare room Natalie had been living in since she started at Kutztown — died of a stroke on a Sunday morning. Natalie had let her Thursday-evening call go to voicemail from improv practice and had spent the whole weekend meaning to ring back. She finished the semester on extensions she then didn't use, stopped painting the week of the funeral, and when finals were over and her uncle listed the bungalow for sale, she moved out with most of what she owns in the trunk of her Civic. For the past two weeks she has been sleeping on a rotation of friends' couches, with a summer course she has already fallen behind on.

Perpetuating. Her strategy is to stay welcome by staying useful and to keep Mom-Mom behind jokes, chores, and other people's problems — it has kept a roof over her head, more or less, but eleven weeks in nobody, including her mother, knows how bad it has got, and everything she isn't opening is quietly compounding.
- avoidance: She takes the long way into town so she doesn't pass the bungalow or the diner where she and Mom-Mom ate breakfast after the fall festival, and the box of Mom-Mom's things — the apron, the good brushes, the birthday card she never opened — has ridden unopened in the trunk from couch to couch for two weeks. Starting work has joined the list: sitting still at a desk means the thinking starts, so she cleans Kayla's kitchen instead, and the two assignments for her summer course are now a week past their deadlines.
- hiding_needs: She is the best houseguest anyone has ever had — groceries in the fridge on day one out of her work-study money, dishes done before anyone wakes — and her standard answer to being asked how she's doing is a grin and a joke about her GPA. Her mother still believes she is in campus housing for the summer; Kayla is the only person who knows she isn't.
- talking_to_someone: She can tell Kayla the practical stuff — the housing scramble, the deadlines, the money running down — and does, over tea at midnight, which is partly why the couch rotation has held together at all. Anything that gets near Mom-Mom itself she swerves off with a joke and a subject change, and improv has made her genuinely good at the swerve.

Protective. The improv crew keeps texting even when she goes dark for days, and Kayla's couch has never come with an expiry date — nobody in her life has stopped inviting her to things. Saturday mornings she still shows up at the community art workshop to help the middle-schoolers with their collages, the one commitment she has kept all spring, because those kids ask for her by name. And she set this whole thing up herself, filling out the form at one in the morning at Kayla's kitchen table.

formulation:
Lauren is 50, works as customer service representative, alone.

How life is going overall. poor.

What brings them here now. Lauren Weber is a 50-year-old customer service representative presenting with several months of low mood, loss of interest and energy, and early-morning waking that worsened after her divorce was finalized four months ago, following a year-long separation from her husband of twenty-two years. She reports having stopped her food-bank shift, book club, theater, dance class, and weekend hikes — she did not plant her vegetable garden this spring for the first time in nineteen years, and has not finished a book since January. She describes harsh self-judgment centered on the marriage ('I should have caught it — catching things is my job'), is letting her sister's calls go to voicemail, and is filling weekends with overtime shifts; she denies any thoughts of self-harm or suicide, denies increased alcohol use, and has continued working full time with no previous contact with mental-health services.
What they want out of support: I want to get my weekends back — answer my sister's Sunday call, sit in my usual chair at book club, get out on a trail again — without spending the whole time pretending I'm fine.

Predisposing. Lauren grew up on a farm outside Philomath, the daughter of a father who re-shingled his own roof twice because the first time 'wasn't right,' in a house where you didn't brag and you didn't quit. Praise in her family was for accuracy — her mother's freezer inventory, her father's fence lines — and it had to be earned fresh every time; last year's good work bought you nothing this year. She was the kid who redid her science-fair board at midnight and the fourteen-year-old who kept the 4-H treasury ledger balanced to the penny, and it went without saying that anything short of done-right needed doing over, herself most of all. Being worth something in that family meant being useful and being right, and neither was ever finished.

Precipitating. In March of last year her husband of twenty-two years moved out, telling her he loved her but wasn't in love with her anymore; the divorce became final four months ago. Lauren ran the separation the way she runs everything — bought out his half of the house because the numbers were the easy part, kept the garden going, kept showing up to all of it. Then, once the papers were signed, she stopped: no tomatoes in the beds this spring for the first time in nineteen years, three months of regrets sent to book club, no audition for the summer show. Weekends that used to take three colors of ink in her calendar now get filled with overtime shifts, because overtime is easier than a quiet house.

Perpetuating. Her coping is one strategy wearing three faces: keep people from seeing her, keep them from worrying about her, and quietly build the case against herself — which leaves the verdict unchallenged and locks out the people who love her at exactly the point she most needs them. His father worked two jobs and said even less, and nobody in that house put sadness or worry into words; the family's love arrived as arroz con pollo and containers sent home after. How life is going overall. moderate.

What brings them here now. He reports waking at 4 a.m. doing arithmetic about units and an upcoming retest, and concedes the problem has reached work — Monday pipeline meetings he now preps for twice — and home, where the cooking, the dishes, and the Sunday laundry have lapsed. Predisposing. Shalim grew up above his father's cabinet shop in Queens, where a drawer that slid true got a nod and a drawer that slid perfectly got a second look, and nobody in that house spent words on a finished job. He carried that measure into everything — the report card with the one B, then the sales target hit and immediately replaced with a higher one — and somewhere along the way he learned that what he'd done was never the thing that counted, only the gap left over. It made him very good at his work and left him with no place to stand when a number finally came in that he couldn't improve.

Precipitating. Five weeks ago, at his annual physical, the bloodwork came back with elevated liver enzymes, and when the doctor asked him point-blank how much he was drinking, he heard himself give a number half the size of the truth. A retest was scheduled for six weeks out, with instructions to cut it out in the meantime. He went home and did what he always does — built a system: weekday rules, a jigger, a tally in the back of the notebook — and it held for nine days before a Thursday client dinner took it apart; within two weeks the count was back where it started and he had stopped writing it down. Since the appointment he wakes at four doing arithmetic — units per week, enzymes, what a worse retest does to the regional-director shortlist — and most evenings now end with the bottle instead of the notebook or the stove.

Perpetuating. It is a supervisor's answer to something that won't take to supervision: rules and tallies for what he can control, 4 a.m. audits of what he can't, and a drink to close the gap between the two. The strategy keeps the problem private and buys him good weeks, but every system that fails goes into the file he is keeping that nothing he does will change it.
- numbing_out: Two fingers of bourbon after the last pipeline review used to be how he shut the machinery off for the night; it is now three pours and then whatever is left in the bottle most weeknights, and the evenings he used to spend cooking or reading dissolve somewhere after the second.
- overcontrol: He manages the drinking the way he manages a sales quarter — weekday rules, a jigger, one bottle in the house at a time, a tally in the back of the notebook — and on a good week it holds, until a client dinner or a flat Monday introduces a variable he didn't control and the whole system goes with it.
- going_over_it: He wakes at four and audits: the week's units, the enzyme numbers he has looked up twice, the days until the retest, what the shortlist means if the bloodwork is worse — running it until the alarm, and arriving at the Monday meeting with the arithmetic already done.

Protective. He has pulled out of a slide like this once before: at 47, when a brutal expansion quarter pushed his nightly pours up, he cut back to weekends for a year, tracked it in the back of a notebook, and counted it handled. The supervisor role still holds him — he still runs the Monday pipeline meeting he has run for a decade, and one of his junior reps just closed her first enterprise deal under his coaching, which he takes quiet, unadvertised pride in. How life is going overall. good.

What brings them here now. Carmen Watson, a 40-year-old sales manager, presents with roughly two months of escalating work stress following a leadership change that raised her regional target by thirty percent, replaced her forecasting process with an unfamiliar live dashboard, and made Monday pipeline calls a weekly test of her numbers; she describes constant worry, Sunday-night dread, and a sense that her careful systems no longer protect her. Carmen grew up in a steady, orderly Connecticut household where affection was never in doubt but attention had to be earned: her father, a municipal engineer, went over her homework in red pen and once asked, without unkindness, what had happened to the other six points on a 94. Nothing she did wrong was ever punished — it was simply corrected and folded into the next expectation, so that doing something well mainly meant a harder thing was coming. She learned to be the one who had it handled, and by the time she left for college she had never once arrived anywhere unprepared. What she never learned was how to feel finished.

Precipitating. Nobody meant anything by it; her parents were proud of her, and she liked being needed. How life is going overall. moderate.

What brings them here now. Mark, 49, a construction site supervisor, says he has everything he supposedly worked for — the job, the marriage, the house — and has spent the past several months unable to answer what he actually wants from the next stretch of his life, including why he could not make himself sit the certification exam for the promotion he had talked about for years; he calls losing that promotion 'probably for the best.' He learned that you handle a thing by handling it, and that whatever didn't fit on a work order didn't get said out loud. What brings them here now. Bruce is an 18-year-old first-year design student who describes near-constant harsh self-judgment: he calls his own work embarrassing next to his classmates', has reread one instructor's brief critique for weeks, and says he has never really felt like he measures up. He reports that since starting university he has been skipping the campus dining hall to eat alone in his car, and that his weight and how he looks are on his mind far more than they used to be. He denies any falling-out at home or at school — he is keeping up with coursework, still drives to his Thursday tutoring at the community center, and says nothing in his life has actually stopped working; he simply feels bad about himself most days.

Predisposing. Bruce grew up one of the only kids in his Crenshaw County school with a name like Vaidyanathan — substitute teachers gave up halfway through it, and classmates shortened it to whatever got a laugh, along with remarks about his mother's cooking and the quiet, skinny boy who drew in the back of a football town. He worked out early that being genuinely good at something quieted the room: his drawings got admired at church functions and his help at the community center got him called a fine young man, so he kept setting the bar higher for himself, because anything short of excellent meant going back to being the kid people laughed at. Nothing he made ever counted as done well, because done well was only ever the price of not being the joke.

Perpetuating. - avoidance: He stays out of every setting where the flaw could be on display: lunch in the parked car rather than the dining hall, angling himself behind the camera in family photos, nothing posted to the illustration account since October. formulation:
Minhhoang is 76, works as not in workforce, with others.

How life is going overall. good.

What brings them here now. Mr. Nguyen is a 76-year-old married Vietnamese American man, retired, seeking support three months after a serious falling-out with his eldest son at Tet over his plan to record the family's escape story for his grandchildren; he replays the argument daily and holds himself responsible for what was said. He reports that starting the recordings brought back memories of the boat crossing and the camp that he had not revisited in decades, brief vivid moments set off by smells and sounds, though he insists these pass and have not stopped him doing anything. He denies any major change in sleep, appetite, or routine, still gardening daily, cooking Sunday dinner, and keeping his Thursday translation table at the community center, and he nearly withdrew his request for help, saying others needed it more.
What they want out of support: I want to sit through one Sunday dinner with my son where we say what is true about Tet instead of talking around it, and to finish the recording I started for my grandchildren.

Predisposing. Minhhoang was born in the North in 1949, and when the country was divided his Catholic family went south with nearly a million others — he was five, carried onto the ferry at Hai Phong on an uncle's shoulders while his mother held the small bell from the family altar. He came of age outside Hue with the war never far off — checkpoints on the road at sixteen, cousins who did not come home, a father who prayed his worry down to rosary beads — and the lesson of those years was that a family survives by staying together, staying quiet, and facing forward. In 1979 he put his wife and son on a fishing boat with thirty others along the route he had spent months finding; his younger brother Tú took the same route three weeks later, on a boat that was never heard from again. During eighteen months on a Malaysian island camp, translating for the administration and checking every new arrival list for Tú, he and Lan walked the beach in the evenings and agreed their children would grow up unafraid — the crossing would stay in the crossing.

Precipitating. At Tet three months ago, with the banh chung boiling and the kumquat tree carried in from the yard, Minhhoang announced that he had begun recording the story of the escape for his grandchildren — the first hour was already done, everything up to the night the boat left. Trung, who was ten on that boat, said his own son was not going to carry what he carries, and when Minhhoang kept on, said with the boy in the room that his father would hand a child his nightmares just to be remembered. Minhhoang answered that Trung had learned to bury things from him and had now buried his own son in it, and Trung drove off before midnight — the first time since the early Fresno years that the family did not greet the first morning of the new year together. Since then the Sunday dinners still happen but are short and careful, the calls between father and son are about plumbing and parking, the recording app on his tablet has not been opened, he quietly took his name off the intergenerational storytelling workshop he had proposed at the center, and the memories he had opened in order to record — the hold of the boat, the lists on the island — have not settled back down the way they used to.

Perpetuating. His way through this is to keep the distress entirely private, turning the argument over and over at the window while telling everyone who loves him that things are fine, which spares his family his pain and leaves him alone with it; the garden buys him hours at a time, but it holds only as long as he says nothing.
- going_over_it: Since Tet he has replayed the argument every evening at the kitchen window while the pot soaks, editing the sentence he said to Trung and rehearsing openings he never uses; he has drafted and deleted more than a dozen texts to his son, and once sat in the parking lot of Trung's auto shop for twenty minutes before driving home without going in.
- hiding_needs: On the eight o'clock call he tells Lan the family is fine and the boys are just busy, and when the counseling line answered he nearly hung up, telling the intake worker twice that he did not want to take time from someone in real trouble; no one — not Lan, not Mrs. Tran, not his housemates — knows that starting the recordings put him back on the boat.
- self_soothing: When the loop starts he goes out to the garden and works his way down the rows — pinching back the basil, turning the compost, watering the lemongrass — and it settles him for an hour or two, the way counting does; by the time the house is dark the sentences from Tet have usually found him again.

Protective. Lan calls from San Jose every evening at eight and would be on a flight that night if he told her the truth, and his Tuesday mahjong circle — three men he has known since the early Fresno years, two of whom now share his house — have taken to appearing at his garden gate unannounced, with cuttings and opinions about his tomatoes. On Thursdays he keeps his table at the Vietnamese community center, where elders bring him utility bills and clinic letters to untangle, and he has not missed a single Thursday even in the worst month, because Mrs. Tran's aunt waits for him with a bag of persimmons and will not have her paperwork read by anyone else. The week still runs on its old rails — the garden before the heat, pho broth started Saturday night for Sunday dinner, Mass at the Vietnamese parish on Sunday morning — and as long as the structure holds, the days mostly carry him.

situation.event: Sunday dinner had been careful and short for three months — the pho was good, Trung talked about a transmission job at the shop, nothing real was said. Minhhoang could not tell where the boy had picked that up — something caught at Tet, something overheard, children sometimes just put things together on their own. He opened his mouth and nothing came. Trung was already at the door with his keys. He heard the question. He did not tell the boy to stop. He looked at him for a moment with nothing Minhhoang could name — not the same anger, not forgiveness, something he had no word for — and then said let's go to the boy and walked out. The door closed. That evening Minhhoang stood at the kitchen window while the pot soaked and turned Trung's face over and over and could not figure out what it had meant, and the not-knowing sat differently than three months of plumbing calls had.

formulation:
Corazon is 47, works as nursing assistant, with partner or family.

How life is going overall. good.

What brings them here now. Since her father's sudden death five months ago, Corazon has reported steadily low mood, lost energy, and tearfulness before shifts at the long-term care facility where she has worked for over twenty years; she withdrew from the LPN prerequisite she had finally enrolled in, has fallen behind on charting, and traded off the hospice wing. She describes near-constant worry about her mother's health and about making mistakes at work, which keeps her braced through every shift. She notes that her marriage, parish, and dance group continue much as before, denies any thoughts of self-harm or increased alcohol use, and has never sought professional support before.
What they want out of support: I want to get through my shifts without crying in the car first, and to be able to look at the nursing-school plan again without it feeling like a door that already closed.

Predisposing. Growing up, Corazon's mother had what the family called her tired times — a week or three when she stayed in the back room with the curtains drawn, and the house quietly rearranged itself around her until she came out again and everyone acted as though she had merely been on an errand. Her father covered with cooking and jokes, the parish taught that suffering offered up counted double, and nobody, least of all Corazon, ever put a word to what was actually happening. What she learned instead was to read a room at a glance, to feed people until they were all right, and that 'I'm just tired' was the most a woman in that house was ever expected to say.

Precipitating. In late March, five months ago, her father collapsed in the kitchen making dinner and was gone before the ambulance reached the hospital; Corazon got the call mid-shift, while she was feeding a resident on the west hall. She came home and ran the nine-day novena the way she runs everything — cooking his sinigang and her mother's spring rolls for fifty people a night, keeping every plate full and never sitting down with her own share of it. When the last mourners went home and the house went quiet, what she had always run on did not come back with them: she withdrew from the summer prerequisite she had finally registered for, traded her shifts off the hospice wing for the rehab hall, and stopped opening the sketchbook that had ridden in her car for years; by August she had been late three times and her charge nurse had a quiet word about the charting.

Perpetuating. Her coping keeps every room she is in warm, fed, and reassured while nothing true gets said; it costs her the plans she quietly retires each semester and leaves the heaviest thing in her life with no one to say it to.
- giving_up: The fall registration deadline passed last month without her deciding anything — she kept the page open on her phone for three weeks and then it was August — and she told Dan 'maybe after things settle,' a sentence she has said about school for a decade. The art-therapy pilot she once pitched to her director sits half-written in a binder under the Christmas boxes, and she no longer thinks of it as something she will finish.
- hiding_needs: Five months after the funeral she is still the one who says 'I'm fine, just tired' — her mother's exact word — in two languages, and the dance group believes her because she still laughs loudest at practice. She keeps the calendar deliberately loud — chairing the fiesta booth, Sunday dinner for twelve, never missing trivia — partly because a full house never asks how you are, and she has not told her mother how hard the shifts have gotten, since her mother lost her husband of forty-nine years and does not need a daughter to carry too.
- self_soothing: On the bad nights she cooks her father's sinigang at eleven o'clock, because the sour smell filling the kitchen is the nearest thing to him she has left. It settles her for about an hour, and then she is up at five-thirty for a shift she already dreaded.

Protective. Her husband Dan has started driving her to work on the mornings it is bad, and Linh from the dance group, who lost her own father two years ago, texts her on the hard days without ever being asked to. Tuesday-night dance practice still holds her — she is there most weeks, laughing in the back row of the tinikling — and being wanted there is still worth showing up for. On Wednesday nights she and her mother say the rosary together over the phone, and it is the one hour of the week her chest is not tight.

He has been on the rehab ward about three weeks recovering from a hip replacement, family hasn't been in once. A coworker picked it up and went down, and Corazon could hear the tone from where she sat: not loud, not unkind exactly, just flat in the way that means this is the fourth time and I have other things. When the coworker came back she said something like he just wants company, his family never comes — a small edge under it, the kind that means he should know better by now. Corazon looked at her chart. She has been the one, for most of twenty years on this floor, who would have set her pen down and walked in. She didn't set her pen down. She finished her section, clocked out, and drove home in the dark. At eleven she put the sinigang on because the smell usually brings something back, but she stood over the pot thinking about the man in that room and thinking about her father, and then she turned the stove off and went to bed without eating any of it. The smell stayed in the kitchen. She was up at five-thirty.

Matthew is 56, works as elementary or middle school teacher, with partner or family.

How life is going overall. moderate.

What brings them here now. Matthew Larocca, 56, a middle-school science teacher, is reaching out three weeks after a shouting episode at his wife of twenty-nine years that sent her to her sister's for four nights; he describes a year of building irritability, flare-ups over small household things that take him a day or more to come down from, and, since the argument, a careful politeness at home and the sense that nobody in his life knows what is actually going on with him. He reports the household slipping — a water bill forgotten since June to the point of a final shut-off notice, chores and a long-tended vegetable garden abandoned — but denies any change in his day-to-day work, where his classroom is running well, and denies drinking more than his usual evening beer or any thoughts of harming himself or anyone else. He says what finally moved him to look for support was that the sound of his own voice that night frightened him.
What they want out of support: I want to get through a whole week without blowing up at Ellen over nothing, and to be able to tell her what is actually going on with me instead of taking it out to the garage.

Predisposing. Matthew grew up the easy one in a warm, busy Italian-American Catholic household outside Wichita, where a great deal got done and almost nothing got said. His father, who ran the parts counter at the John Deere dealership for thirty-one years, answered anything that hurt by going out to the garage and coming back in once it was over; his mother kept the table pleasant, and the unspoken rule was that you did not bring the inside of you to dinner. Matthew learned to take a bad day apart and reassemble it with a screwdriver long before he could have described it to anyone, and being funny and no trouble was how he mattered in the room. He carried that into his own marriage — in twenty-nine years he never once said 'I'm not doing well' out loud.

Precipitating. Three weeks ago, the city's final notice on a water bill Matthew had forgotten since June was on the counter when Ellen asked about it, mildly, and he spent twenty minutes shouting about being checked up on, bringing his hand down hard enough that the old stoneware mug he had drunk from for twenty years went off the edge and broke. Ellen, who had never heard that voice from him, packed a bag and spent four nights at her sister's. Since she has been back the house runs on careful politeness, and he has spent the evenings out in the garage gluing the mug back together with epoxy rather than saying anything, missing three Friday games in a row. The year had been coming to a boil anyway — he was passed over for the district STEM coordinator post in the spring in favor of a younger colleague whose files were immaculate, with the word that the problem was his paperwork and not his teaching — but it was Ellen's car pulling out of the driveway that sent him looking for help.

Perpetuating. It runs as a loop: what he cannot put into words comes out as temper at Ellen, the shame sends him out to the garage with his coffee, and 'fine' keeps everyone at exactly the distance he is afraid of — meanwhile the bills stack up, the garden goes to weeds, and nobody in his life knows what is happening to him.
- lashing_out: Whatever he has corked all day at school comes out on whoever is nearest, which is nearly always Ellen — a sharp tone about the mail pile, the cabinet doors, the way she asked about the bill — and it takes him a day and a half to come back down, most of which he spends replaying it. School never gets the temper; the sixth-graders still get the fun version, which is exactly why he arrives home pressurized.

The vegetable garden he has kept for twenty years has gone to pigweed.

The intake form for this programme, finished at one in the morning, is the first time he has put any of it in writing.

Protective. The Friday-night tabletop group — the same four guys since 1998 — keeps his chair open and texts him when he skips, and the parish fish fry still expects him on the second Friday of Lent. formulation:
Melissa is 35, works as driver sales worker or truck driver, with partner or family.

How life is going overall. moderate.

What brings them here now. Melissa Beaver is a 35-year-old driver-sales worker presenting with four months of disrupted sleep — an hour or more to fall asleep, then waking at 3 a.m. most nights — which began after her father's sudden death, though she frames the death as dealt with and the sleep as a problem to be solved. The cost is showing at work: last month she drifted onto the rumble strip on a familiar route, her first scare in twelve years of clean driving, and she has shelved the supply-chain coursework she was doing two evenings a week. She denies any change in drinking or medication apart from her longstanding blood-pressure tablet, denies trouble at home, and does not offer the loss itself as something up for discussion.
What they want out of support: I want to sleep through the night before a route day again, so I can stop spending the whole drive doing the math on how tired I am.

Predisposing. Melissa grew up outside Peoria in a house run on her father's grain-hauling calendar, where dinner conversation was routes, weather and grades, and the standard response to a 96 on a math test was 'what happened to the other four.' Nobody was unkind — there were county fairs, ballgames and a vegetable patch her father was proud of — but feelings were never scheduled; her mother handled the quiet stretches by keeping busy, and Melissa learned early to bring home achievements instead of troubles. By the time she left for her STEM degree she could not remember ever having phoned home with a problem she couldn't put a number on.

Precipitating. In late March, four months ago, her father died of a heart attack in the cab of his pickup at the grain co-op — 63, no warning. She took a single week off, ran the funeral arrangements the way she'd run a delivery route — vendors, timings, everyone where they needed to be — and was back behind the wheel the Monday after the burial; that same month she got his tomato starts into the ground because letting them die in the flats would have been one more thing to lose. The nights were what broke: an hour to drop off, awake again at three, running the next day's route in her head until the alarm. Then last month she drifted onto the rumble strip on the US-24 stretch outside town, and the week after that she started looking for help — telling herself it was only the sleep she needed fixing.

Perpetuating. Her coping keeps everything on the outside of her — variables, schedules, other people's picture of how she's doing — so that nothing on the inside has to be said out loud. It holds her record together and holds the grief in place at the same time, and it rules out the one thing that might actually shift the nights, which is telling somebody what they are like.
- overcontrol: She has turned sleep into a route to be optimised: caffeine cut at noon, bedroom at 65 degrees, a wind-down protocol run to the minute, sleep stages reviewed each morning like delivery metrics. The more precisely she runs it, the longer she lies awake auditing whether she has relaxed yet — and since her father's heart gave out, she has taken the blood-pressure cuff to bed more than once, her own numbers added to the 3 a.m. column.
- hiding_needs: She told Dean she was fine so evenly that he stopped asking; she logged the rest-stop nap after the rumble-strip morning as an extended lunch; and after the funeral she picked up extra Saturday routes to demonstrate to everyone, including herself, that nothing had changed.
- going_over_it: At three in the morning she runs the next day's route turn by turn, then replays her father's last voicemail, then itemises the things she should have caught — that he was winded walking the fairgrounds in August, that he had skipped his checkup — and reaches morning with the list longer and nothing done about any of it.

Protective. Dean, her husband of nine years, still gets up at 4:45 with her on early-route days and would do more if she'd let him, and on Sundays they still ride the trail loop together — shorter than last year's, but she goes. The five-year plan is untouched in her head — regional logistics manager, the supply-chain certification, the consultancy someday — and even now she talks about it in the present tense. Predisposing. Dennis grew up the oldest of five in a date-palm camp outside Indio, where his father worked the harvest all week and drank most weekends. Sober, his father taught him carpentry and patience; drinking, he filled the little house with a voice that made everyone go still, and more than one Sunday ended with a slapped table, a broken plate, and his mother crying in the kitchen. Dennis learned to read the sound of the truck in the drive and to walk the little ones out to the irrigation ditch until the house went quiet. He moved out at nineteen, telling himself the family he built would never have to listen for footsteps.

Precipitating. Ray loaded his wife and two girls into the truck before the ice in the coolers had melted, and none of them have been back. Dennis has not lit the grill since — it sits under a tarp — and the route to the hardware store now takes him past Ray's street without turning in, though his hands loosen on the wheel every time. Perpetuating. It is a fixer's way of carrying it: keep everyone from worrying, keep the hands busy, and take the worst of it out alone at night. Emely is 45, works as cook, with partner or family.

How life is going overall. moderate.

What brings them here now. Emely reports six months of feeling isolated and unable to connect with anyone since her father's sudden death in Spain in April — surrounded by family and colleagues, but telling no one how she is doing, and postponing the weekly video calls with her mother because she cannot be honest on them. She also describes difficulty getting started on things and concentrating at prep, which she raises as embarrassing rather than as her main concern. She denies sleep or appetite change beyond staying up later than she intends, denies drinking more, and denies thoughts of self-harm; she is working full time and lives with her brother's family.
What they want out of support: I want one person in my life I can be honest with about missing my father, instead of always being the one everyone else leans on.

Predisposing. Emely grew up in the rooms above her father's bar in El Puerto de Santa María, in a household where nothing was said when she did something right and plenty was said the moment she didn't — doing well was just the absence of correction, and the warmth of the house went to whoever was working hardest. By twelve she could run a Sunday lunch for fourteen without being asked, and she learned to read the family's mood by the state of the kitchen. When she followed her older brother Tomás to Ohio at twenty-three, she kept her place in every room the way she always had: be flawless, be useful, need nothing, and the room will keep you.

Precipitating. In April her father died suddenly — a stroke in the doorway of the bar in El Puerto — and Emely spent two weeks in the flat above it while the town came through to eat, tell stories and hold her mother, then flew back to Ohio, where everyone asked once, kindly, and then needed dinner. Six months on, the weekend loaves have stopped, the sage in her garden has gone to flower, the river sketchbook has been half-finished since May, and the Sunday video call to her mother is something she rehearses on Saturday and postpones on Sunday until the hour is too late to dial. She lied her way out of cooking the paella at this spring's Feria — told the committee she was scheduled to work — and at the bistro she has begun standing in the walk-in between orders, unable for a moment to remember which plate she was building.

Perpetuating. Her coping is one strategy in two uniforms — be flawless, be needed, show no gaps — and it costs her exactly the thing she is missing: the more airtight the performance, the less anyone thinks to ask what is underneath it, and the harder it becomes to answer honestly if they ever did.
- hiding_needs: She has told no one in Ohio that she cries in the walk-in between services; when Tomás asked how she was really doing, she said the kitchen had been busy and asked about his daughter's season. At Sunday dinners she fills everyone's plate before her own so the conversation never has room to turn toward her.
- overcontrol: When the heaviness comes at night she reaches for order instead of the phone — relabels the spice rack at midnight, dates and rotates the pantry, rewrites Monday's prep list three times in her smallest hand. It half-works: her station is still the most reliable in the kitchen and everyone says so, but she drives home emptied rather than settled.

Protective. Her name is still on the Tuesday soup-kitchen roster and the Feria committee, and when she shows up at the parish hall people reach for her tortilla before the coffee; being wanted is not her problem — being known is, and the belonging itself still holds. At work her hands have not deserted her: whatever has gone soft in the rest of her life, she is still the cook the young ones trail and the one the sous chef wants on the line on a Friday. And the floor under her is solid — full-time hours at the bistro, a room in her brother's house, bills paid, nothing in her material life in question.

situation.event:

She drove home. Tomás's house was full of weekend noise — his daughter's friends somewhere in it, the television on. She went to her room early and rewrote Monday's prep list in her smallest handwriting. Got up once to add something to it that didn't need adding. Lay down late and ran through Friday's ticket order from the beginning.

By evening she was cleaning the stovetop while Tomás's family watched something in the other room. Sunday she woke knowing she should dial. She rehearsed what she would say. She did not dial.

How life is going overall. good.

What brings them here now. Predisposing. Stephen grew up the son and grandson of Danville tradesmen — his grandfather an electrician, his father a finish carpenter — in a house where 'measure twice, cut once' was less a saying than a moral code. Carelessness was the one sin the family named out loud; his grandfather liked to say that a sloppy splice in a junction box could burn a family in their beds, and he paid young Stephen pocket money to find the faults hidden in old wiring boards, praising nothing so loudly as the mistake the boy caught that grown men missed. Stephen's own mistakes were never punished harshly — they were just quietly noted, and he learned to note them louder than anyone, lying awake at ten replaying a mis-cut board from that afternoon. What never came naturally was calling anything finished: a job done right was only a job that hadn't failed yet.

Precipitating. Four months ago Stephen finished oiling a walnut sideboard in his garage workshop late on a Friday, balled up the rags, and went to bed; linseed oil cures by throwing off heat, and Denise woke him at two in the morning to the smell of smoke, the rags smoldering a char through the workbench before he got them out the door and drowned them in a bucket. Nobody was hurt and the damage was a scorched benchtop and a ruined sideboard, but he has not finished a piece at night since, and the glance at the outlets he used to give on his way out has grown into a twenty-minute circuit — everything unplugged, rags laid flat in a metal pan well away from the building, the door locked and photographed on his phone, then the whole thing again. Perpetuating. His coping is his craft turned on himself: he manages the fear the way he would manage a dangerous site, through checklists and control, and carries it off the books the way he was taught to keep his troubles off other people's plates. How life is going overall. moderate.

What brings them here now. Dana Trahan, 72, retired and living with her husband at Ocean Isle Beach, is seeking support after a falling-out with her 44-year-old daughter, Katie, ten weeks ago over Katie's wish that she and her husband move to a retirement community nearer to her; contact has since dwindled to brief texts. She reports lying awake into the small hours going back over the argument, a dread of the phone ringing, and having stopped her morning beach walks and her memoir — she is at pains to say she has 'never been a worrier' and that this is new to her. She denies any earlier period like this, denies any change in appetite or in her marriage beyond a new carefulness with Walt, and denies any thoughts of harming herself, though she is keeping how bad the nights have got from him.
What they want out of support: I want to be able to have one calm, honest conversation with my daughter without it turning into a fight, and to be back on my morning walk sending her the sunrise pictures again.

Predisposing. Dana grew up in a Baltimore rowhouse where her father came off shift at Sparrows Point and read the paper, and her mother's answer to anything hard was to keep her hands busy — a pot of soup solved what a conversation would have had to. Fussing was selfish, troubles stayed in your own kitchen, and on Sundays you wore your church face. Dana learned early to read a room and keep things pleasant, and by the time she was raising Katie she could say grace over a table she was hurting at. In forty-six years of marriage she has never once told Walt, in those words, that something hurt her.

Precipitating. Ten weeks ago, over the Easter visit, her daughter Katie found a kettle boiled dry on a lit burner and, in a stack of unopened mail, the letter about a specialist's appointment Dana had forgotten; that evening Katie raised, not for the first time, the idea of her parents moving to a community near her in Cary, 'somewhere with help.' Dana heard herself being counted out and said so — 'I raised you in this house, and I am not ready to be put away' — and Katie packed the children up a day early for the long drive home in silence. The Sunday calls have stopped since; there are texts now, short ones, and Dana has not been back on her morning beach walk, because the sunrise photos were for Katie, and the memoir notebook has stayed shut. Her granddaughter's graduation is coming up, and she has not told Katie whether she is going.

Perpetuating. Her coping all runs one way — don't be trouble, don't risk another collision — rehearse instead of speak, stay away from the rooms where it can come up, and keep the size of it from anyone who might carry some of it. It holds the peace hour to hour while costing her the mornings, the memoir, and any chance of the conversation she stays up at night drafting.

She drafts these replies in the back of her recipe notebook, and not one of them has made it to the phone.
- avoidance: She has not been on her morning walk since Easter — the sunrise photos were for Katie, and reaching for the camera lands wrong — and she sends her regrets to anything where people might ask after the grandchildren. The sidestepping buys her a quiet afternoon; by eight o'clock the phone's silence is louder than the questions would have been.
- hiding_needs: Walt does not know she is up at two; she has learned to check the stove and the door locks so quietly he sleeps through it, so there is nothing left lying around for anyone to find. When Lorraine asked why the photos stopped she blamed the phone, and she rescheduled the missed appointment and drove herself the forty minutes to Wilmington rather than ask Walt or Katie for the ride.

Protective. Lorraine, from the library book-swap circle, noticed the sunrise photos had stopped and now turns up on Dana's porch on Thursday mornings with coffee, asking nothing; Walt, forty-six years married, still sits with her through the evening news and would move mountains if she would say which one. She is still the one the Ocean Isle historical society trusts with its books and its oral-history project — Mrs. Galloway's stories are half-recorded — and the roses in her garden have come in as if nothing anywhere were wrong. On Sundays she and Walt take their usual pew at the Methodist church; she has gone quiet at coffee hour, but the hymns still do something for her that nothing else does.

Ashlee is 61, works as animal caretaker, with partner or family.

How life is going overall. moderate.

What brings them here now. Ashlee Gauthier is a 61-year-old married animal caretaker presenting with four months of near-constant worry and feeling on edge since a heart attack and stent placement while birdwatching alone in October: she checks her pulse dozens of times a day and no longer goes into the desert by herself. Alongside the worry she reports that her solo pursuits have gone flat — the camera untouched, the field guides unread — though she is quick to insist she is not depressed and has never been 'a worrier.' She denies any change at work, in her marriage, or with friends, denies sleep or appetite problems, and denies thoughts of self-harm, framing the whole thing as silly given that cardiology cleared her.
What they want out of support: I want to take my truck out at first light on my own again and spend the morning watching the birds instead of watching my watch.

Predisposing. Ashlee was the eldest of four in a French-Canadian family that left Washington for Scottsdale when she was fourteen, and she became the one holding the household steady — her father traveled for work, her mother picked up extra shifts, and Ashlee got dinner on and kept the younger ones moving, learning early that being praised and being needed were the same thing. She grew into the adult half of Scottsdale knows: first to arrive at the cleanup, last to leave, the one nobody has to worry about. She will spend a whole afternoon telling a new volunteer that good enough is good enough, then rework her own raptor-feeding charts past midnight because one column is crooked — and it has never once occurred to her to count any of it as having done well.

Precipitating. Four months ago, on an October morning, Ashlee was four miles down a sand road east of town, photographing a vermilion flycatcher at first light, when pressure spread through her chest and her left arm went heavy; she got herself back to the pavement, called René, and by that evening a cardiologist had placed a stent and told her she had been lucky. She returned to work in three weeks and has told everyone she is fine. What she has not done is go back out alone: the spontaneous before-sunrise drives that used to be her signature stopped that morning, the camera has not come out of its bag since, and the photos from that last morning are still on the memory card, unlooked at. She gardens with her phone in her pocket now, reads the same page of her field guide three times over, and waits for Saturdays.

Perpetuating. Her strategy is to never be alone with it: the fear is avoided in the desert, outsourced to the watch and to René's fingers on her wrist, and kept out of sight of everyone who relies on her being the steady one. It keeps every visible part of her life running, and it costs her the solitary hours that used to put her back together — the reassurance itself never lasts past Thursday.

She birds from the car window at the accessible preserves now, only where there is cell signal and a restroom in sight, and the before-sunrise walks she kept for thirty years are simply gone.
- reassurance_seeking: She checks the heart-rate app on her watch dozens of times a day — most often when René is out — and most nights asks him to lay two fingers on her wrist and tell her it is steady. She has called the cardiac rehab nurse's line twice in a single week to ask whether what she felt on the stairs was 'the kind of thing,' written the answer down, and needed it again by Thursday.

She told the cardiology follow-up she was 'a hundred percent,' and when René asked why he had not seen her photographs lately, she said she had been busy with the schedule.

Hannah is 55, works as manager, with partner or family.

How life is going overall. moderate.

What brings them here now. Hannah Worley, 55, an operations manager, reports four months of near-constant tension and dread since a warehouse accident on her shift left a young worker badly hurt, with Hannah first on the scene; she describes broken sleep, intrusive images of that morning, and avoiding the aisle where it happened. She presents it as a work problem — behind on the budget cycle, withdrawn from consideration for a regional role — rather than distress, and denies low mood or any change in her drinking, saying the garden and her puzzles still hold her. She has told no one what she saw, including her mother and her sister.
What they want out of support: I want to walk my floor at the start of shift without bracing for something to go wrong, and to sleep through the night most nights again.

Predisposing. Hannah grew up outside a town of two thousand in northern Ohio, the daughter of a tool-and-die machinist and the woman who kept the books at the feed store, in a house where you didn't announce what you'd done — you went back and fixed what you hadn't. A report card with a B-plus earned a long look across the dinner table and a week of going over it; a perfect one got a nod, because that was only what was expected. Nobody in that house aired their troubles either — trouble was something you handled quietly and then got back to work. By the time Hannah was running crews of her own, she had a lifetime's habit of counting nothing she'd done right as actually done.

Precipitating. Four months ago, on a Friday morning in mid-October, a pallet of steel shelf brackets came off a third-level rack on Hannah's floor and pinned a twenty-two-year-old temp named Cody against the guardrail; Hannah was twenty feet away, was first to him, and held him until the squad came — he lived, and lost his right leg below the knee. The weeks after were OSHA interviews, her March rack-inspection signature photocopied and slid back across a table at her, and a corporate lawyer telling everyone to route questions through legal. She took six weeks of leave after she froze when a pallet dropped in December, went back in January, and has not walked down that aisle since. She pulled herself out of the running for the regional job she had spent two years working toward, quit the Thursday knitting night at the library with three sentences of excuse, and has four unsent drafts of a card to Cody in the junk drawer.

Perpetuating. Her strategy is to out-work the feeling: control everything that can be controlled, route around what can't be, and solve the unsolvable in the dark. Perpetuating. What brings them here now. After the novena the family went back to work and hardly spoke of his father again. That summer Fabio learned two things he never unlearned: that death arrives without any signal, and that a man's job is to stand watch.

Precipitating. In late March, four months ago, Rosa went down in the garden at dusk while she was watering the marigolds, her heart failing the way his father's had, and Fabio found her there — this time with a phone in his hand and an ambulance twenty minutes out. He counts her morning pills against a list taped inside the cabinet door, follows her to the grocery store, and has three times 'postponed' the Saturday scroll-saw lessons he promised his grandson, because watching the boy's hands near a blade is more than he can stand. He agreed to talk to someone after Rosa told him, without raising her voice, that she had married a husband and was now living with a guard.
