How life is going overall. good.

What brings them here now. Laura Moore, 72, presents after a falling-out with her younger brother ten weeks ago over the family memoir she wrote and sent him: he objected to its account of their father's drinking and their mother's illness, told her she had never built a family of her own, and has not called since. She reports waking at night to go over the phone call and worrying through the day about an upcoming family graduation party, but denies any change in appetite, energy, or routine — the garden, book club, church circle, and volunteering all continue as before. She has never married, lives alone, and her brother's family is her closest kin.
What they want out of support: I want to be able to have one honest conversation with my brother without it ending the way that phone call did, and to finish the memoir without feeling I've betrayed somebody either way.

Predisposing. Laura was fourteen when her mother's health turned, and from one winter to the next she was the one running the bungalow outside Detroit — cooking off the envelope of grocery money, minding seven-year-old Gerald, keeping track of her father's shift schedule so supper was ready either way. In that house you counted your blessings out loud and kept the rest to yourself: nobody asked anybody how they were doing with any of it, and nothing got said that couldn't be said over a casserole. Laura got so good at that arithmetic that her own life became the thing that could wait, and by the time she looked up, the man she'd been stepping out with had married someone else and she was the family's steady sister, aunt, and driver.

Precipitating. In March, after three years of writing, Laura had the family memoir bound — two hundred pages running from the Irish great-grandparents to the bungalow — and mailed copies to her brother Gerald and each of his three children. Gerald phoned three days later: the chapters on their father's drinking through the layoff winters and on their mother's long illness were, he said, private matters nobody had asked to see in print, and a woman who never built a family of her own had no business deciding what theirs meant. The Sunday-night calls have stopped since, and she has not been out to his place, though everything else still runs — the garden, the book club, the circle. Two weeks ago Erin's graduation invitation came, and she has read it a dozen times, twice hunting for her reading glasses, and still cannot say out loud whether she will walk into that party.

Perpetuating. It is a closed loop: nights for going over it, days for showing nobody, and the needles and the hoe buying an hour's quiet at a time. It keeps her functioning and keeps everyone comfortable, at the price of Gerald never learning she is hurt — so there is nothing for him to answer, and the rift sits exactly where March left it.

- hiding_needs: She has told Dot she's fine, just sleeping poorly, and she has written Gerald five letters and mailed none of them, because she won't have him thinking she's after pity. When Erin calls on Sundays, Laura steers the talk to the girl's plans and away from anything that would show her hand.
- self_soothing: When the worry gets loud she knits — three scarves since the phone call, given away as fast as she finishes them — and on the bad nights she is out in the vegetable rows by six, weeding in the cool, which settles her for an hour or two before the thinking starts up again.

Protective. The Tuesday knitting circle at St. Brigid's still saves her the seat by the window, and Dot, who has sat beside her there for eleven years, noticed within two weeks that something was wrong and kept after her until she made this call. Her youngest niece, Erin, sent a photo of the memoir with a note that it was the first time anyone had told her grandmother's story, and still rings on Sunday evenings when her father isn't home. Laura has promised the library's volunteer coordinator she'll train the new crop of shelvers in September, and she has already picked out yarn for the digital storytelling class she means to take in the fall — the last chapter isn't finished, and she has not stopped meaning to finish it.

How life is going overall. moderate.

What brings them here now. Bernice is a 30-year-old stylist presenting with stress and overwhelm rather than low mood: since her mother's stroke four months ago she has been running her mother's care — pills, appointments, groceries, insurance forms — alongside a full client column, and the strain is showing at work, where she has begun double-booking clients and the paperwork for the salon she wants to open sits untouched. She frames the problem as 'not enough of me to go around' and is tearful at times, but denies feeling depressed, denies losing her enjoyment of the work when she is behind the chair, and denies any conflict with her partner, her roommates or her mother. She is quick to shrug the caregiving off as 'just what you do,' though it now takes most of her evenings and weekends.
What they want out of support: I want to get through a normal week — clients seen, Mama's appointments covered, the salon paperwork actually done — without lying awake at two in the morning listing everything I've dropped.

Predisposing. Bernice grew up the bright, arty one in a practical Murfreesboro household where effort had two settings, done and not done: her father supervised a line at the Nissan plant in Smyrna and had no patience for almost, and her mother, the busiest helper at their church, loved loudly — but loudest when Bernice was impressive, at the honor roll, the piano recital, the kitchen-table up-dos she did for half the youth group. Nobody was ever unkind about it; they didn't have to be, because Bernice took over the grading herself — a B got a polite nod where an A got warmth, a friend's crooked homecoming up-do was 'perfect, sweetheart,' and her own got redone twice. By the time she left for Middle Tennessee State she was carrying a rule she had never once said out loud: anything short of extraordinary didn't count as done, and nothing she finished was finished enough to sit down and enjoy.

Precipitating. Four months ago, in early March, Bernice's mother had a stroke at the kitchen table of the house Bernice grew up in, and after five weeks of hospitals and rehab in Nashville she came home unable to drive, with a slow left hand and a Sunday pill box she cannot manage alone. With her older brother in Chicago only able to call on Sundays, the driving, the cardiology and physical therapy appointments, the groceries and the insurance forms all landed on Bernice, squeezed into the gaps between clients. Since then she has quietly dropped out of the master-colorist certification course she had already paid toward, given up her Tuesday gallery nights and Thursday yoga, and stopped opening the notebook where she was sketching the floor plan of her own salon; last month she double-booked two brides for the same Saturday and had to hand one over to a stylist she does not trust with an up-do. A fortnight ago she sat crying in her car between a balayage and her mother's pharmacy run, and that is when she started looking for somewhere to talk.

Perpetuating. Bernice copes by managing the audience: keep the show dazzling, keep the needs invisible, and paint over whatever is left. It keeps the room warm and the chair full, and it costs her the help standing right in front of her, because nobody can offer to carry what they cannot see, and every 'I'm fine' makes the next one harder to take back.
- hiding_needs: When a regular at the shampoo bowl asks how she is really doing, she has a bit ready — a joke, a hair flip, 'busy is a blessing, sugar' — and her partner and her brother in Chicago both get 'I'm fine' and 'we've got it handled' so reliably that they have mostly stopped offering more. What she hides is not the busyness, which everyone can see, but the crying in the car and how close the salon notebook is to being put away for good.
- distraction: When the pile gets loud — the salon loan paperwork, her mother's insurance forms, the callbacks she owes — she opens the watercolors instead, or starts a board for the next costume party, and surfaces at one in the morning with three color studies finished and every envelope still sealed. It half-works: the painting is the one thing that still feels entirely hers and it genuinely settles her, but the pile never shrinks, and the nights it works are getting further apart.
- reassurance_seeking: After a wedding she refreshes the salon's Instagram to watch the likes land on her up-dos, texts the bride 'any photos yet??' and rereads the reply three times, and fishes with the junior stylists — 'be honest, was the copper too warm?' A full row of hearts and she can sleep that night; a quiet post and she is up late redoing the color formula in her head and deciding she is slipping.

Protective. She isn't short of people: her partner of five years has quietly taken over the Wednesday grocery run and her laundry without ever being asked, her two roommates leave soup on her shelf with her name on it, her best friend from her Middle Tennessee State days texts every Sunday no matter how long Bernice has gone without answering, and two of the junior stylists have started covering her lunch slots without making a thing of it. The work itself still holds her up — brides are booked into the fall, clients ask for her by name, and she still privately believes she does the best color in Rutherford County, which happens to be true. A couple of nights a week she still gets the watercolors out at the kitchen table after the house has gone quiet, and it is the one hour where her head goes quiet too, and she remembers she is an artist and not just an errand list.

The week had been the same shape as every week since March: a full client column, her mother's appointments squeezed into the gaps — cardiology, physical therapy, the pharmacy run — and the pile of sealed envelopes on the kitchen counter quietly growing. She had drawn that page on a winter night feeling like someone who was genuinely about to do something.

She stood there holding it. Then she closed it and put it back under the pile. She didn't open the watercolors either. She sat at the table with the sealed envelopes still around her, and eventually went to bed.

Joshua is 74, works as not in workforce, alone.

How life is going overall. good.

What brings them here now. Joshua York, 74, reports ongoing distress three months after two men forced their way into his garage, held him down on his kitchen floor, and robbed him; he describes waking at two and four in the morning re-running the event, checking locks repeatedly, leaving lights burning all night, and a startle response when approached from behind. He insists his days are unchanged — bridge, Rotary, the garden, the incubator bookkeeping — and denies low mood, appetite change, or heavier drinking, though he admits the evenings 'got quiet.' Alongside this he is questioning whether he is still the right man for the mentoring and board roles he had pencilled in for spring, wondering aloud whether at his age he should be 'starting things or winding down.'
What they want out of support: I want to sit on my own patio at dusk without listening for the gate, sleep a night through without walking the house, and decide whether that book of mine is still worth writing.

Predisposing. Joshua grew up outside Davenport, Iowa in the fifties, eldest of three in a farmhouse where the supper rule was that you reported what you'd done, not how you felt. His father, a plant foreman home from the war, treated worry like weather — something you noted and worked around — and his mother's answer to any trouble was 'well, what are you going to do about it?' Joshua learned young to give the status report and keep the rest off the books, and by the time he was running divisions he could narrate any crisis in clean paragraphs without once saying he was afraid. The fear that moved in after September found a house with no words in it.

Precipitating. In late September, three months ago, two men followed Joshua through the open garage door of the house he'd shared with his late wife, took him down onto the kitchen floor as he set the last of the season's tomatoes on the counter, and held him there — a forearm across his neck, ninety seconds by his count — while they took his wallet, his phone, and the engraved watch from his retirement dinner. He was back at bridge that Thursday with the story shaped into comedy, and the daytime ledger has held: Rotary lunches, the garden, the incubator bookkeeping, all running as before. But the evenings went — he stopped sitting on the patio at dusk, the hour it happened — and he now leaves the kitchen light burning till morning and wakes at two and four with the ninety seconds running. When a Rotarian he's known twenty years clapped him on the shoulder from behind a few weeks back and he came up out of his chair heart pounding, he decided whatever this was wasn't leaving on its own, and made the call.

Perpetuating. Joshua manages the outside of the thing and keeps the inside of it off the books: control every variable, tell no one, fill the hours. It keeps his days looking normal from across the street, but it means the ninety seconds have never been told to anyone who could help him set them down, so they keep arriving at two in the morning looking for a variable he hasn't checked yet.
- overcontrol: The man who ran operations runs the house like an audit: cameras he installed himself over a weekend, re-keyed deadbolts, a mental log of which neighbors' porch lights come on when, the garage door kept shut mid-carry even with both hands full of tomatoes. At two in the morning he re-runs the ninety seconds hunting for the variable he missed, then gets up and checks a door he has already checked.
- hiding_needs: At the bridge table the robbery is a comedy routine — 'two amateurs, and they left the good scotch' — and when Marv asks how he's really doing, Joshua answers with the insurance claim's progress. His daughter's Sunday texts get photos of the garden and a thumbs-up, never the part about the lights left on.
- distraction: Mornings still work: out at six-thirty with the coffee before the heat, counting birds for the foothills list, and the difficulty can't find room in a day that full. It holds until dusk — which is exactly when it finds him — so he pads the evenings with re-filing photographs and answering old email, and calls it staying busy.

Protective. Marv from the bridge table has taken to calling on Sunday evenings without being asked, and Joshua's daughter in Sacramento texts every week and would drive down in a night if he'd let her. Twenty-some years in Clovis Rotary means he still walks into the weekly lunch as 'Joshua York, past president,' the man who chaired the fundraisers, and nobody there treats him as anything less. And the memoir is still real to him — chapter headings on a legal pad in the kitchen drawer, the small-business advising pencilled in for spring — a future he keeps arguing for even on mornings he wonders whether he's too old to be planning one.

How life is going overall. moderate.

What brings them here now. Beverly Odom, a 68-year-old skincare specialist still in full practice, reports four months of near-constant worry and feeling on edge since her husband's heart attack in April, from which he has recovered well: she now checks her phone between clients, wakes at five to watch him sleep, and came in after catching herself reaching for the wrong enzyme strength mid-treatment last month while rereading a text from him. She describes growing friction with her husband since the scare — his skipped cardiac-rehab sessions, the monitoring he experiences as fussing — but denies low mood, panic attacks, appetite or weight change, heavier drinking, and any previous contact with mental-health services, and reports that her garden, knitting, and routines outside work are largely unchanged. She dates the difficulty precisely to April and frames it as a problem of professional standards rather than of health or the marriage.
What they want out of support: I want to get through a full day of clients without once checking my phone or second-guessing my work, and to be able to talk with Glenn about what happened in April without one of us leaving the room.

Predisposing. Beverly grew up on a quiet street outside Marshfield in a house whose weather came from her mother's bad spells — days when the curtains stayed drawn, the doctor made a house call, and the little yellow tablets came out of the vanity dish. Nobody said more about it than 'your mother's nerves are acting up,' and her father's only instruction was not to upset her, so Beverly learned to come in from school, read the kitchen for trouble, and keep everything smooth: supper on time, no surprises, her own troubles folded small and put away. What she took from that house, without ever saying it aloud, was that somebody has to be watching for what's coming, because things come apart when nobody is. Her mother's people were the same way — her grandmother took to her bed for whole seasons — though in that family and that town, nobody ever gave it a name.

Precipitating. In April, four months ago, a receptionist appeared at the door of Beverly's treatment room mid-facial: the neighbor had called — Glenn was in the driveway with chest pain and an ambulance was coming. He was in a cath lab before she reached the hospital; one stent, five days, home again, and the cardiologist has called his numbers excellent at every visit since. Beverly went back to work the following week with her phone silenced in her apron pocket and taken out between every client, and she has not slept past five since; last month, rereading Glenn's text about renting a rototiller instead of the label in her hand, she reached for the wrong strength of enzyme on a client's neck and caught it a breath from applying it. She sat in her car for twenty minutes afterward, and that was when she started looking for someone to talk to.

Perpetuating. Her coping is one strategy wearing three faces: control whatever can be controlled, carry the rest alone, and quiet it down among the rosemary when it gets loud. It carried the house and the practice through the spring, but it costs her the conversation — with Glenn, with anyone — that might actually help, and it is beginning to cost her the attention her clients are paying for.
- overcontrol: Everything within reach gets managed: the weekly pill organizer checked twice on Sunday nights, texts to Glenn at ten and two to confirm the midday medication, treatment rooms prepped an hour before the first client, labels she has known by heart for thirty years read again anyway. It has kept anything from going wrong, at the cost of arriving home from good days spent — and it was the split attention, phone in the apron pocket, that put the wrong bottle in her hand last month.
- hiding_needs: At the hospital she was the organized one — calling their daughter in Springfield, learning the medication schedule before the discharge nurse finished explaining it, telling everyone Glenn was doing really well — and she has kept that answer ever since. When Glenn tried once to talk about the driveway, she got up to finish the dishes; her sister-in-law asked how Beverly herself was doing and got his latest numbers.
- self_soothing: In the hour before dark she is out with the herb beds, and she has told the rosemary things she has not said to anyone with a pulse — the two a.m. audits, the argument she didn't have, the twenty minutes in the car. Four scarves since spring, rows she can count. It settles an evening and buys her the sleep until five; it gets her no closer to saying any of it where it would count.

Protective. Glenn is still the one who notices her — last week he set her watercolor pad out on the kitchen table without a word about how long it had sat in the closet — and even the arguments they have had since April happen inside a marriage of forty years, not at the edge of one. At the spa she is still the person the two junior estheticians bring their puzzling cases to, texting her photographs at nine at night, and being needed that way steadies her more than she lets on. And she has somewhere she is going: the shelves of labeled infusion jars in the spare room, the half-written guide on skin health for older adults, the workshop she promised the community center in October — a life after the treatment room that she has already started building.

Lee is 58, works as machinist, alone.

How life is going overall. moderate.

What brings them here now. Lee is a 58-year-old machinist presenting with five months of mounting work pressure that he describes as being 'in over my head for the first time in my life': since his shop lost two of its five machinists he has been covering extra machines, quoting, and training their replacements on six-day weeks, and the strain shows at home — a shut-off notice on the power bill, dishes and groceries gone by the wayside — and in his relationships, where he has stopped fishing with his oldest friend and gone quiet on his sister. He denies low mood ('tired, not sad'), denies that his two-beer evenings are a problem, and denies any thoughts of harming himself. He has never sought any kind of support before, and reached out after standing at his sculpture bench for an hour, tools in reach, unable to begin.
What they want out of support: I want to get back on top of the house and the bills, and have my Saturdays feel like mine again — fishing with Walt, the volunteer workshop, my sculpture bench — instead of spending them braced for Monday.

Predisposing. Lee grew up in Kent in a house that ran on shift work: his father cycled between the shipyard and sleep, and after his younger brother was born his mother was never quite well again. Lee was sweeping floors at a Renton machine shop for under-the-table cash by thirteen, and the summer he finished eighth grade he didn't go back to school — he started at the shop full-time instead, handing his envelope across the kitchen table to his mother every Friday. Nobody in that house asked a boy how he was managing any of it; you worked, you didn't complain, and whatever came up got carried. He has been the one carrying things ever since.

Precipitating. Five months ago the shop lost two of its five machinists in the same month — one retired, one moved to Everett — just as an aerospace subcontract landed, and the owner asked Lee to cover the open machines, take over the quoting, and train the two twenty-year-olds hired to fill the gap. Lee said sure before the sentence was finished, and has been on six-day weeks since, getting home past seven with nothing left. The house has gone in the meantime — dishes sit in the sink for a week, the fridge is down to beer and mustard because real grocery runs stopped somewhere in month two, and a few weeks ago the power bill went unpaid long enough to draw a shut-off notice, the first missed payment of his adult life. He stopped answering Walt's texts about Sunday fishing, let the fall enrollment deadline for the CNC programming course he'd been planning around for a year pass without signing up, and the kinetic sculpture he's been building for two years sits untouched under a shop towel; what finally pushed him to ask for help was standing at that bench one Saturday for an hour, tools in reach, unable to begin.

Perpetuating. It is one strategy in three parts: absorb everything where people can see, disappear from anyone who might notice the strain, and turn the volume up at night until his head goes quiet. It has kept him the man everyone leans on for forty years, and it is exactly what is burying him now — nobody knows, so nobody helps, and the pile only grows.

- withdrawal: He stopped answering Walt's texts about Sunday fishing, telling himself he'll call when things ease up, and quietly stepped back from the Saturday workshop rather than explain why he couldn't keep up with it anymore.
- numbing_out: Most nights he gets in past seven, opens a couple of Rainiers, and puts a record on loud enough to run the job list out of his head; it does get him to sleep, but the evenings blur together and the stack of mail keeps migrating from table to counter unopened.

The teaching is one: an hour spent showing the new hires how to square a vise or read a micrometer is still the best hour of his day, and the community workshop he volunteers at would take him back the moment he walked through the door. His hands are another — whatever else is sliding, work at the bench still comes out right, and after thirty-five years he trusts that completely. Since then she and her husband exchange little beyond logistics, the Sunday family dinners and this year's Diwali hosting have stopped, and unopened bills are gathering in a study drawer. She calls the whole thing 'a misunderstanding that got loud once,' insists her husband is a good man and her daughter is simply busy, and reports that her three days a week at the practice, her health, her friendships, and her sleep are all unaffected — no one outside the house, she says, has noticed a thing.
What they want out of support: I want Sunday dinner back — my husband and my daughter around my table again, with nobody being careful around each other.

Predisposing. Kalpanaben grew up in a joint-family house in Ahmedabad that ran on hospitality — thirty plates at Navratri, a bed always made up for whichever uncle arrived from the mill towns — and she was the daughter who could be counted on to keep it all warm. Nobody was ever unkind; it simply never occurred to anyone to ask her what was wrong, because whatever was wrong went to the kitchen with her and came out sweetened and served. She learned to read a room perfectly and to say nothing about herself in it, and by the time she married Ramesh at twenty-nine and followed him to Cambridge three years later, she was fluent in other people's comfort and wordless about her own.

Precipitating. Ramesh retired from his engineering firm eighteen months ago, and the small slips that had always been part of Kalpanaben — the insurance renewal she meant to chase, the autopay she had been meaning to set up since spring — came under his full-time attention for the first time in nearly forty years. Two months ago a red final notice from the electric company beat her to the mailbox, and the argument that night was the worst of their marriage: he said he could not count on her for the simplest things, and she found nothing to say back. A week later Priya, who had been making her own dentist appointments since she was fourteen, said what she had apparently been saving up for years — that the whole family had spent a lifetime quietly covering for her mother — and the Sunday dinners stopped that week. Diwali came last month, and for the first time in thirty-five years Kalpanaben did not host: Priya held it in Somerville, Kalpanaben arrived with shop-bought sweets, and she has spent most evenings since out on the terrace with her seed catalogues and her paints, letting her daughter's calls ring through to voicemail.

Perpetuating. Her way through is to keep everyone comfortable and the trouble out of sight — smooth the surface, hide the notices, tend the pots — and it does keep the house quiet, but the drawer fills, the family stays at arm's length, and the distance she fears asking for anything would create is being created instead by her silence.
- hiding_needs: She has told no one — not her sister on the Sunday video call, not the book club, not her mentees — that anything is wrong at home; the calls stay on recipes and the granddaughter, and when anyone asks how Ramesh is finding retirement she says 'busy being useful' and turns the talk to a building.
- avoidance: She keeps away from the places the trouble lives: the study desk where the envelopes stack up — each new final notice goes into the drawer with the others, unopened — and the kitchen in the early evening while Ramesh is in it; on the bad days Priya's calls ring out, and she answers by text about the granddaughter instead.
- self_soothing: When the house goes quiet she takes her tea out to the terrace with the seed catalogues and her watercolours, and an hour with the winter pots or a painting of last month's Diwali lights settles her more than anything else does — it is the one stretch of the day she is not drafting sentences she will never say, though it holds her for less time each week.

Protective. Three days a week she still goes in to the small Cambridge practice where she is a senior designer, and it is the one place the last two months have not touched: the young architects she mentors bring their models and their problems to her desk, and she is entirely herself there. The rest of her week keeps its shape — the terrace pots in the early morning, book club on Thursdays, yoga on Saturdays, the long camera walk past the old brick terraces — and she keeps those appointments even in the weeks when home is hardest. And she got herself here: at sixty-seven, having told no one else in her life that anything is wrong, she found this support on her own, filled in the form, and turned up.

It is late November in Cambridge, the evenings closing in and the terrace pots ready to come inside. Her three days at the practice went steadily — a junior architect brought her a site-section problem that needed real thought, and she gave it. Thursday book club came and went; she brought something, the evening was what it was. Home has been what it has been for two months: logistics with Ramesh, the kitchen managed in shifts, the study drawer she has not opened.

On Wednesday evening Priya put a voice note on the family thread. The granddaughter had said her first real word — said it clearly, said it twice — and Priya's voice in the recording had that lit-up quality it gets. Kalpanaben listened to it standing in the kitchen doorway, then took her phone out to the terrace and played it again in the cold. She typed 'clever girl!' with a heart and sent it. Priya replied with a thumbs-up, and that was the whole exchange.

Sunday passed without a dinner. Ramesh cooked and she ate alone at the table with a seed catalogue, the house quiet in a way she cannot get used to. Afterwards she took her tea out to the terrace and stayed there in the dark and the cold. She has not rung Priya.

Britto is 32, works as retail salesperson, with partner or family.

How life is going overall. moderate.

What brings them here now. Britto Desai, 32, presents following a falling-out with his father three months ago, after an arranged match his parents had spent the winter setting up ended when the other family went quiet following a lunch at which his career plans came up; the house has been cold since, and he has withdrawn from family contact, taking closing shifts to miss dinner, ignoring his aunt's calls, and deflecting his sister. He describes himself as 'the family's loose end' and is harsh about being thirty-two, unmarried, and 'still on the floor,' though he is clear that none of this has touched his work, where he continues to train new hires and is regarded as one of the stronger salespeople. He denies drinking to cope or any change in sleep or appetite; his evenings go to cooking and strategy games, later than he would like.
What they want out of support: I want to be able to sit through Sunday dinner without anyone leaving the table early, and without spending the hour before it rehearsing what to say if the marriage questions start.

Predisposing. Britto grew up in a house in Fort Bend County where love was never in short supply but approval had to be earned. His father, who had arrived in Houston with two suitcases and a chemistry degree nobody would recognise, kept a quiet mental ledger of the family's children — the pharmacist cousin, the niece who made partner before thirty, Britto's own older sister now running a dental practice in Dallas — and his mother relayed the community's arithmetic gently, over dinner. A ninety-four on a report card earned 'and what happened to the other six points,' and being good at something unmeasured, like cooking, was a nice hobby rather than a credit. Britto learned to scan a room for disappointment before he had finished his sentence, and concluded that being loved and being assessed were the same activity.

Precipitating. Three months ago, a match his parents had spent the winter arranging — a primary school teacher from a temple family, four meetings over two months — quietly ended when her family stopped returning calls a few days after a Sunday lunch where Britto, asked where he saw himself in five years, said honestly that he loved retail and hoped to make supervisor. Two days later his father pressed him about the unfinished degree again and Britto, who had never raised his voice in that house, did; the argument finished with his father saying 'you're thirty-two, figure it out,' and the house has been polite and frozen since. Britto picked up closing shifts so he is still behind the register when the family sits down to dinner, eats in his room when the timing does not work, and has stopped answering his aunt's Sunday calls. He signed up for support two weeks before Diwali, after his mother asked him to please just look happy in front of the relatives.

Perpetuating. Britto's coping is distance plus busyness: stay out of the rooms where the questions get asked, keep his hands full, and tell anyone who checks in that everything's fine. It buys him quiet evenings, but his absence reads to his family as sulking — which hands his father one more thing to be disappointed about — and it means that three months on, no one in his life has heard a single true sentence about what happened.
- withdrawal: He volunteered for closing shifts for most of the last month so he would still be at work during family dinner, and he leaves Saturday cricket as soon as the last over is bowled — the after-match table is where the phones come out and somebody always asks how 'the marriage thing' is going. He still helps at the temple food drive, but he stays in the kitchen where nobody asks him anything.
- hiding_needs: His sister gets ten minutes about her clinic and her in-laws; he has never told her about the match, the lunch, or the thing their father said, because she 'married out of that house and shouldn't have to carry it back in.' When his cricket captain asked last month if he was okay, he said work was busy and steered the conversation to the fixtures.
- distraction: Late at night he cooks for one — a full pot of rajma, a new regional recipe — because chopping is the only thing that stops the replay of that Sunday lunch, and then it is strategy games until one in the morning, one more turn, one more turn. It works while his hands are busy and stops the moment the stove is off; twice this month he has nearly missed Sunday warm-ups.

Protective. His sister calls every other Sunday whether he has anything to say or not, and his cricket captain of six years has taken to walking him to his car after matches to check in. At the store he is still the person the manager hands new hires to train, and last month a customer asked for him by name; he has held onto that. The cooking and the cricket have not stopped either — he plays every Saturday, partly because skipping would raise more questions than going.

formulation:
Doris is 65, works as occupational therapist, with partner or family.

How life is going overall. moderate.

What brings them here now. Doris Buzzi is a 65-year-old occupational therapist who reports constant worry and physical tension since her husband's heart attack five months ago: she lies awake listening to his breathing, rechecks his medications, and has stopped attending her Thursday book club and family Sunday dinners. She also describes trouble getting started and concentrating — the adaptive-equipment workshop she had planned has been postponed twice, the quilt she began in the winter is untouched, and she rereads the same page without taking it in. She denies panic attacks, denies feeling low or losing pleasure in her garden and sunrise walks, and insists her client work has not slipped, though she concedes that no one at work or in her family knows how rough the nights have been.
What they want out of support: By the end of this, I want to be able to sit through a book club evening or a Sunday dinner at my daughter's without checking my phone every few minutes, and to get through a night without lying awake counting his breaths.

Predisposing. Doris was the eldest of four and the family's English from the time she was small: at eleven she rode the bus with her mother to the county clinic to translate, and it was Doris who had to carry the cardiologist's words about her abuela's failing heart home, softening them in Spanish so her mother wouldn't cry on the ride. The grown-ups praised her for being so helpful, so mature; nobody asked what it was like to be the one holding the news. She learned early that in her family somebody has to be watching, listening for the cough through the wall — and that the somebody was her.

Precipitating. Five months ago, in the middle of a May night, Doris woke to the sound of Ruben struggling to breathe and drove alone behind the ambulance down Highway 288 to the hospital in Lake Jackson; he came home nine days later with two stents and a prognosis the cardiologist called excellent. She kept everything running at first — work, meals, the garden — but she hasn't been back to Thursday book club since June, and after sitting through Father's Day at Marisol's with her phone face-up on her thigh and leaving before the flan, she has begged off family Sundays altogether. The first of the adaptive-equipment workshops she'd been planning since last winter has been postponed twice, and she is already talking herself into handing Marisol the Día de los Muertos altar this year — the first time in twenty years she wouldn't build it herself. She still walks the beach at sunrise, but the walks have gotten shorter, the phone warm in her hand.

Perpetuating. The strategy is to run a tight ship and keep the crew calm: control every variable, cancel every absence, and let nobody see the cost. It has taken the book club, the family Sundays, most of her sleep, and the workshop plans that were supposed to be her next chapter, and it has left Ruben with a wife who is never far away and never quite there.
- overcontrol: She has rebuilt the household into something like a cardiac unit: a seven-day pill organizer checked twice against the pharmacy list, low-sodium meals cooked ahead and labeled by day, and she walks the cardiologist's prescribed half-mile beside Ruben every evening with her phone timer running, though the cardiologist told her plainly the walking was his to do. Each new system buys her a day or two of ease, and then she starts scanning for the next variable that isn't pinned down yet.
- avoidance: Anything that puts evening, distance, or a weak phone signal between her and Ruben quietly falls off the calendar: book club Thursdays (she told Rosa the drive had gotten tiring), the seniors' health fair where she used to run a table, the drive to Houston. She still says yes to things and then finds a reason the day before — a headache, a delivery, the weather — and has nearly finished talking herself into giving Marisol the altar this year.
- hiding_needs: Nobody at work knows; when Rosa texts to check on her she types back 'todo bien, just tired,' and when Ruben asks how she slept she says 'fine.' She waits out the small hours with a virtual museum tour running with the sound low so it won't wake him, and tells herself he doesn't need to know how many times she has counted his breaths — frightening him feels like the one thing she can still protect him from.

Protective. Rosa, her comadre of thirty years, still saves her a seat at book club and texts every Thursday whether Doris comes or not, and her daughter Marisol calls from Houston on her evening commute with no agenda, just to talk. Ruben is recovering well — walking, joking, back to his woodwork — and knows more about the bad nights than anyone, though even he gets the rounded-down version. At work she is still the one the junior therapists bring their hardest cases to, and she has not missed a single client session through any of this. And she has been somewhere like this before: after her father died in 2009 she spent the better part of a year checking locks and sleeping in snatches, and it lifted — slowly, but it lifted — which is some part of why she believes this will too.

situation.event: Tuesday was Ruben's five-month cardiology follow-up. Doris had moved an afternoon client to be there. His brother offered to drive him the day before, and Ruben said she didn't need to come — just a routine check. She said fine. She worked the empty slot. He came back in good spirits: excellent recovery, the cardiologist had said; the sodium restrictions could ease up gradually; the medications were being managed well. Ruben mentioned, not to wound her, that he'd told the doctor Doris had been on top of everything, and the cardiologist had said to make sure she was getting out and doing her own things. Ruben delivered this at the kitchen table as good news, as permission. She said that's great and moved to the dishes. When he went out to the shed she stood at the counter looking at the labeled containers in the fridge — Monday through Wednesday — and the twice-checked pill organizer beside the sink. She stood there for a while. She didn't call Rosa. She didn't call Marisol. Before she went to bed she checked the pill organizer again, already knowing it was right.
